subject: biology
title: Characteristics and kingdoms of living organisms
key_idea: All living organisms share the same set of characteristics. Scientists sort them into groups using features that can be seen or tested, and a dichotomous key does this one yes or no question at a time. Viruses have no cells and are not counted as living.

blocks.text: Every living organism carries out the same set of processes. This section gives each one a clear meaning.

items.meaning: An action by an organism, or part of it, that causes a change of position or place.
The chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism.
The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment.
A permanent increase in size and dry mass.
The processes that make more of the same kind of organism.
The removal of the waste products of metabolism and of substances in excess of requirements.
Taking in materials for energy, growth and development.

items: The first letters spell **MRS GREN**: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition.
Plants move parts of themselves, for example a shoot growing towards light.
Excretion is not the same as egestion. Egestion is the removal of undigested food, which was never part of the cells' chemistry.
All living organisms show all seven characteristics.
Respiration releases energy. Excretion removes metabolic waste.
Growth is a permanent increase in size and dry mass.

blocks.text: A dichotomous key identifies an organism by a series of questions. Each question has two answers and each answer leads on to a name or to the next question.

items: Use features that can be seen, such as the number of legs, the body covering or the leaf shape.
Use features that do not change, not size or colour, which vary within one species.
Each question must give exactly two choices.
To construct a key, split the group in two on one feature, then split each half again until every organism has its own name.

items.text: Has legs: go to 2. 1b. Has no legs: earthworm.
Has six legs: housefly. 2b. Has eight legs: spider.

items: Start at the first question and follow the answer that fits the specimen.
A specimen with eight legs is a spider.
Every question in a dichotomous key has two answers.
Use clear features that can be observed and that do not vary.

blocks.text: Animals are split into groups using features that can be observed. This section covers the main vertebrate and arthropod groups.

rows: Young are fed on milk from mammary glands. Most give birth to live young. External ears.
Wings and a beak. Lay eggs with hard shells.
Lay eggs with soft shells on land. Breathe with lungs.
Eggs laid in water. Larvae have gills and adults have lungs. Gas exchange also happens through the skin.
Gills for gas exchange and fins for swimming. Eggs laid in water.

items: All arthropods have an **exoskeleton**, a segmented body and jointed legs.
**Myriapods** (centipedes, millipedes): many body segments, each with legs. No wings.
**Insects**: six legs, three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen) and antennae. Most have wings.
**Arachnids** (spiders, scorpions): eight legs and two body parts. No antennae and no wings.
**Crustaceans** (crabs, shrimps): five or more pairs of legs, two pairs of antennae and a hard exoskeleton.
Vertebrates have a backbone. Arthropods have an exoskeleton and jointed legs.
Insects have six legs. Arachnids have eight and no antennae.
Match the features given to the group, then name the group.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Every organism belongs to one of five kingdoms. This section gives the features that place an organism in each.

rows: Make their own food by photosynthesis
Usually a mycelium of threads called hyphae. Some are single-celled (yeast)
Secrete enzymes onto food and absorb the products (saprotrophic)
Single-celled, no nucleus. Circular DNA and plasmids
Most feed on other organisms. A few photosynthesise
Amoeba feeds like an animal. Chlorella photosynthesises like a plant

items: **Ferns**: have leaves called fronds, no flowers and reproduce by spores.
**Flowering plants** have flowers and make seeds. They split into monocotyledons and dicotyledons.

rows: A main (tap) root with side roots
In multiples of four or five

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Statements about cells and feeding are sorted into three groups: animal, plant and fungus.
diagram.prompt: Sort each feature into the kingdom it identifies.

items.text: Has nervous co-ordination and can usually move from place to place
Body is a mycelium of hyphae
Secretes enzymes onto food and absorbs the products

items: Cellulose wall and chloroplasts: plant. Chitin wall and hyphae: fungus.
Prokaryotes have no nucleus. Protoctists are single-celled with a nucleus.
Ferns have spores and no flowers. Dicotyledons have two seed leaves.

blocks.text: Viruses are not cells and are not usually treated as living. This section covers what they are made of.

items: A virus has a **protein coat** around its genetic material, which is either DNA or RNA.
It has no cell membrane, cytoplasm or nucleus.
It is smaller than a bacterium.
It can reproduce only inside a living host cell, so it is parasitic. It can infect every type of living organism.
It does not grow, respire or excrete.

diagram.alt: A table comparing a virus and a bacterium. A virus is smaller, has a protein coat and no cell structure, and reproduces only inside host cells. A bacterium is a single cell with a cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm and a circular chromosome, and can reproduce on its own.
items: Virus
Bacterium
A virus is a protein coat around genetic material.
Viruses reproduce only inside living cells, so they are not living organisms.

checks.q: State what is meant by excretion.
checks.a: The removal of the waste products of metabolism and of substances in excess of requirements.

checks.q: A small animal has eight legs, two body parts and no antennae. Name the group it belongs to.
(Supplement) A single-celled organism has chloroplasts, a cell wall and a nucleus. Name its kingdom.

worked_example.question: Describe two identifying features of monocotyledons.
answer_points: Flower parts in multiples of three.
Vascular bundles scattered throughout the stem.
worked_example.tip: Any two score one mark each. Give features that can be observed.

worked_example.question: Viruses are pathogens but not living organisms. Give three differences between the structure of viruses and bacteria.
answer_points: Viruses have no cytoplasm, organelles, ribosomes or vacuole.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. Say which organism each feature belongs to.

blocks.text: This course adds two more characteristics of life, and names examples for each group.

items: Living organisms also **control their internal conditions** (homeostasis).
Plants store carbohydrate as starch or sucrose. Animals and fungi often store it as glycogen.
Animals usually have nervous co-ordination and can move from place to place.

items.meaning: An organism that causes disease. Pathogens may be fungi, bacteria, protoctists or viruses.

rows: Maize (a cereal). Peas or beans (a herbaceous legume).
Lactobacillus bulgaricus (rod-shaped, makes yoghurt). Pneumococcus (spherical, causes pneumonia).
Tobacco mosaic virus (discolours leaves). Influenza virus (flu). HIV (causes AIDS).
